items.excerpt: Epic Games has sold ArtStation and Sketchfab to KitBash3D, and game artists are openly celebrating — 'free from Epic and their love of AI slop' — after years of complaints that AI-generated art flooded the portfolio site and 3D marketplace. The handover reopens the question of how the industry's main game-art portfolio platform will police generative AI listings.

Epic divests ArtStation and Sketchfab to KitBash as it refocuses on Unreal Engine 6, Fortnite and its developer ecosystem. KitBash co-CEO Banks Boutté frames the deal around creator trust: 'These are platforms where people have built portfolios, careers, and communities.'

With Twitch refusing to build its own AI-use labeling system, streamers are inventing one themselves — tagging channels #AIOptedOut, #NoAI and #NoGenAI so viewers can find creators who pulled their work out of Amazon's training pipeline. It's a grassroots disclosure standard emerging from the creator side rather than the platform.

Twitch streamers discovered their streams, VODs and chat were enrolled in Amazon's AI training by default, and are circulating opt-out instructions plus an 'aioptedout' tag. Twitch's chief product officer conceded the design rationale out loud: 'If it was opt in, nobody would opt in.'

Twitch's new generative-AI training system sweeps streams, VODs and comments into Amazon's models with opt-out defaults, and creators have to actively dig into settings to leave. PC Gamer walks through what the setting actually covers for people whose livelihood is the footage being harvested.

Game Developer's read on Twitch's opt-out AI training: creator-made content is being treated as default training data for Amazon, with no meaningful consent step for the people producing it. The piece frames it as a precedent for every platform that hosts creative work made by game and streaming creators.

Twitch says the quiet part out loud about why its Amazon AI training program is opt-out: 'nobody would opt in.' The admission crystallizes how platforms are sourcing creative training data from the people who make their content.

Amazon is folding Twitch streams and VODs into generative-AI training, the origin report that set off the week's creator backlash. For streamers and game creators it turns years of archived performance work into model fuel by default.

Dean Takahashi asks how outsourcing and co-development studios — the backbone of AAA art and production pipelines — will actually deploy AI tools for their publisher clients as the ecosystem contracts. The column reframes the AI question from 'will it replace devs' to 'who owns the pipeline when the work is external.'

At a KRAFTON x ReLU Games dev talk, the Mimesis team laid out an 'AI game design' methodology: AI should generate new play experiences, not just speed up production. They detailed scrapping the failed Doppelgänger prototype, their Nolan platform for rapid AI-assisted prototyping, and why small purpose-trained networks beat LLMs for a player-mimicking NPC.

Concept art released for Supergirl appears to carry generative-AI tells, reigniting the argument over AI in big-budget character and creature design. The flashpoint is concept art specifically — the stage of the pipeline studios keep insisting is still human-led.
